by Edmund Spenser

It consists of two cantos which were not published in
The Faerie Queen
but assumed to be a part of it.

Spenser was an Elizabethan poet and took it upon himself to write and develop an English literary culture. The main product was the Faerie Queene, written for Queen Elizabeth and her court, hoping to emulate Virgil but firmly set in the Italian mould á la Arioso and Tasso.
In
Mutabilitie
the titaness Mutabilitie interferes with the natural order. Jove attempts to restore the norm.
‘But to the highest Him, that is behight
Father of Gods and Men by equal Might;
To weet, the God of Nature, I appeal.
There-at Jove wexed wroth, and in his Spright’
However, Spenser also wrote a
A view of the state of Ireland
, an imagined dialog during which characters disparage the savage Irish and argue for brutal militarisation of a rebellious land. Eglington was a Presbyterian.

children: The eponymous title character of Yeats' play
Cathleen ni Houlihan
, which Joyce is referencing here, is a poor old woman. Thus, the adjective is, first of all, used disparagingly. With Kathleen symbolising Ireland as a whole, the allusion gains more poignancy.
Beyond that, the county town Wicklow, that was mentioned in the preceding sentence, is called
Cill Mhantáin
in Irish, meaning “church of the toothless one”. The origin of the name is rich in folklore:

“Saint Patrick and some followers are said to have tried to land on Travailahawk beach, to the south of the harbour. Hostile locals attacked them, causing one of Patrick’s party to lose his front teeth. Manntach (toothless one), as he became known, was undeterred and returned to the town, eventually founding a church.” (See:
Wikipedia
The name could, however, also be a toponym and refer to the
St. Patrick’s Church
in Wicklow, which is said to resemble a gappy set of teeth.
Nevertheless, Wicklow and Ireland are superimposed upon each other via the corresponding adjective “gaptoothed”.

By 1868 Mallarmé had come to the conclusion that, although nothing lies beyond reality, within this nothingness lie the essences of perfect forms. The poet’s task is to perceive and crystallize these essences. In so doing, the poet becomes more than a mere descriptive versifier, transposing into poetic form an already existent reality; he becomes a veritable God, creating something from nothing, conjuring up for the reader, as Mallarmé himself put it, “l’absente de tous bouquets”—the ideal flower that is absent from all real bouquets.
